a: the angels of the Lord
p: Where Genesis says "the sons of God," Jubilees says plainly "the angels of the Lord."
b: This verse retells Genesis 6:1-2 and 6:4, where "the sons of God saw that the daughters of humankind were good to look at" (Genesis 6:2). Jubilees settles the old question of who the sons of God were: they were angels. Charles notes that "angels of God" is also how the Septuagint renders Genesis 6:2, and that Philo and Josephus read it the same way. For Jubilees these are the same angels sent down in 4:15 to teach humankind. Here they fall.

a: In a certain year of this jubilee
t: A date, not a timeless myth
p: Even the angels' sin gets a date: a year inside the jubilee named in 4:33.
b: Jubilees dates everything in jubilees of 49 years and in "weeks" of seven years. Here the writer gives only "one year of this jubilee," the twenty-fifth (see 4:33, Noah's marriage). The effect is to set the angels' sin inside ordinary history, as one dated event among others, rather than in a time before time.

a: These were giants
p: Ge'ez räʿayt, "giants": the children of angels and women. Jubilees names three kinds of them in 7:22.
b: Genesis 6:4 says "the Nephilim were on the earth" and calls them "the heroes of ancient times." Jubilees simply says the angels' children "were giants." In 7:22 it gives them a fuller family tree, with the Naphidim, the Naphil and the Elyo. 1 Enoch 7:2 also speaks of giants.

a: All flesh ruined its way
p: Genesis 6:12 says all flesh ruined its way. Jubilees spells it out: people, cattle, wild animals and birds.
b: Genesis 6:12 says that "all flesh had ruined its way on the earth." Jubilees takes it as everything alive and lists the animals one by one. They too "ruined their ways and their order" and began to eat one another, as in 1 Enoch 7:5. This goes beyond Genesis, which does not blame the animals, but it explains why the Flood swept away animals too. Charles points out that later writers took this to mean that different kinds mixed with each other.

a: every thought that the minds of all humankind formed was evil like this all day long
p: This is Genesis 6:5 in Jubilees' words.
b: Genesis 6:5 says that "every plan their hearts shaped was nothing but evil all day long." The Ge'ez says "every thought of the knowledge of all humankind was evil like this all the days." Jubilees keeps the point and adds nothing to it here; the repeat in 7:24 adds "emptiness."

a: Only Noah found favor before his eyes
p: Genesis 6:8: "But Noah found favor in the LORD's eyes." Jubilees adds "only."
b: Ge'ez baḥtitu, "alone," makes the contrast with the rest of the world sharper than Genesis 6:8 does. Jubilees comes back to it in 5:19: no one was shown favor "but Noah alone," and his sons were saved for his sake.
orig: ወኖኅ ባሕቲቱ ረከበ ሞገሰ (wänoḫ baḥtitu räkäbä mogäsä)

a: he told us to bind them in the depths of the earth
p: Genesis never says what happened to the sons of God. Jubilees, with 1 Enoch, Jude and 2 Peter, says they were bound.
b: The "we" is the angels of the presence, who tell this story to Moses (see the book's opening). They themselves bound the guilty angels "in the depths of the earth." In 1 Enoch 10:12 Michael is told to "bind them for seventy generations under the hills of the earth." The New Testament knows the same tradition: God "threw them into Tartarus and handed them over to chains of gloom" (2 Peter 2:4), and "he has kept in everlasting chains down in the gloom, for the judgment of the great day" (Jude 6). This goes beyond Genesis 6, which is silent. Jubilees, 1 Enoch, Jude and 2 Peter share this tradition. The verse ends "bound in their midst and kept apart" (Ge'ez እሱራን ማእከሎሙ ወብሕትዋን (ʾəsuran maʾkälomu wäbḥətwan)), as Charles also renders it.

a: that they be struck down with the sword
p: In 1 Enoch 10:9 the Lord sends the giants against one another; Jubilees tells the same story.
b: Jubilees, like 1 Enoch 10:9, says the giants were not drowned in the Flood but died by the sword, killing one another (5:9). Their fathers had to watch (5:10). In 1 Enoch 10:12 the Watchers are bound "when all their sons have killed one another and they have watched their loved ones destroyed." The two books tell one story, though Jubilees tells it much more briefly.

a: My spirit will not stay on humans forever, since they are flesh
p: Jubilees sets Genesis 6:3 inside the judgment on the giants, so the 120 years can be read as their limit.
b: In Genesis 6:3 the LORD says, "My spirit will not stay in humans forever, since they are flesh. Their days will be 120 years." Readers have long asked whether that means a shorter human lifespan or 120 years until the Flood. Jubilees places the saying between the order to kill the giants (5:7) and the sword sent among them (5:9). Read in that place, the 120 years look like the giants' limit. That reading comes from where Jubilees puts the saying; the verse itself does not say whose days are meant. The patriarchs after the Flood in Jubilees still live far longer than 120 years.

a: the day of the great judgment
p: Jubilees, like 1 Enoch, keeps the guilty angels for a final day of judgment.
b: Charles takes "the day of the great judgment" to be the final judgment, and notes that 1 Enoch 10:12 puts seventy generations between the binding and that day. The same phrase comes back in 10:22 and 9:15. Compare Jude 6, "for the judgment of the great day."

a: He wiped out all of them from their places
p: Do verses 11-16 describe the Flood, or the last judgment? Charles thought the tenses had gone wrong.
b: As the Ge'ez stands, verses 11-12 speak in the past: God wiped them out and made a new nature for all his works. Charles found that hard to believe, since Jubilees itself goes on to show Noah's children sinning again (7:26-27; 10:1). He proposed that verses 10-16 originally described the final judgment, in the future: "he will destroy ... he will make." Other readers keep the past tense: the Flood was a new start, a righteous nature given to creation, which people then spoiled again. The Plain English Translation keeps the tenses of the Ge'ez.

a: a new and righteous nature
p: Claude's theory: Jubilees may see the Flood as a first, partial new creation, a pattern for the final one.
b: This is Claude's suggestion. In 1:29 Jubilees looks forward to "the new creation." Here, after the Flood, God gives "a new and righteous nature" to all his works. If the past tense is original (see the note on 5:11), the writer may see the Flood as a rehearsal of the end: judgment, then a renewed creation that still has to be kept by obedience. Charles took the opposite view and moved these verses into the future. The idea of the Flood as a pattern of the last judgment also appears in 2 Peter 3:5-7.

a: the heavenly tablets
p: Every judgment is already written in heaven. For the term see 3:10.
b: The heavenly tablets are one of Jubilees' key ideas (see 3:10). Here they hold the judgment of every creature, not only Israel's laws. What follows (5:13-18) is a short sermon about judgment set inside the Flood story: nothing is hidden, the judge takes no bribes, and Israel can be forgiven if it turns.

a: in Sheol or in the deep or in the place of darkness
p: Sheol, the world of the dead. Even there, Jubilees says, every judgment is written down.
b: The Ge'ez keeps the Hebrew word siʾol, Sheol. Beside it stand qälay, "the deep" (the waters under the earth, as in 5:24), and mäṣləm, "the place of darkness." The list makes the point of Psalm 139:8: there is nowhere God's judgment does not reach.
orig: ወውስተ ጽልመት ወበሲኦል ወውስተ ቀላይ ወውስተ (wäwsətä ṣəlmät wäbäsiʾol wäwsətä qälay wäwsətä)

a: he does not take gifts
t: The judge who takes no bribes
p: Deuteronomy 10:17 says God shows no partiality and takes no bribe. Jubilees says the same.
b: Ge'ez "he does not lift a face" is the Hebrew idiom for playing favorites, and "he does not take gifts" means bribes. Both come from Deuteronomy 10:17 and 2 Chronicles 19:7. Jubilees adds a picture: even if someone offered "everything on the earth," God would not take it.

a: if they turn to him in righteousness
p: A promise inside the Flood story: Israel can turn back and be forgiven.
b: The angel interrupts the Flood story to speak to Moses' people. Judgment is certain, but "about the children of Israel" a different decree is written: turning back to God brings forgiveness of "all their wrongdoing." This matches the prophets' call to turn (Ezekiel 18:21-23; Joel 2:12-13) and the promise of 1:23, where God will give Israel a new spirit. It is one of the few places in these chapters where Israel itself is in view.

a: once a year
t: The Day of Atonement in the Flood story
p: Charles: "once a year" points to the Day of Atonement, as in Leviticus 16 and Hebrews 9:7.
b: The phrase points to the Day of Atonement, when the high priest went into the holy of holies "once a year, and never without blood" (Hebrews 9:7; compare Leviticus 16:34). Charles notes that Jubilees insists on turning from sin, not on the ritual alone, and compares Mishnah Yoma 8:9, which says the Day does not atone for one who sins planning to repent. Jubilees tells how the Day began in 34:18-19.

a: He showed him favor for the sake of his sons
p: Ge'ez "his face was lifted": God accepted Noah, and his sons were spared for his sake.
b: The phrase "lift the face" is the same idiom used for favoritism in 5:16, but here in its good sense: God accepted Noah. His sons are saved "because of him." Charles compares Abraham's plea for Sodom (Genesis 18:23-32), where the wicked could be spared for the sake of the righteous.

a: in the second jubilee of years
p: The Ge'ez says "in the two jubilee," which cannot fit the book's dates. Charles emended it to "twenty-seventh."
b: Word for word the Ge'ez says "in the two jubilee of years" (በክልኤቱ ኢዮቤልዉ ዓመታት (bäkləʾetu ʾiyobelwu ʿamätat)): a cardinal number where a date needs an ordinal, so "two" may be what is left of a longer number. The Plain English Translation gives it as "the second." By the book's own count Noah was born in the fifteenth jubilee (4:28), so "the second jubilee" cannot be the date of the ark. Charles emended "the reading of all the MSS" to "twenty-seventh," which gives the year 1307 from creation; that year rests on his emendation. He notes that the Samaritan Chronicle also counts 1307 years "from Adam to the Flood." See the variant. Genesis dates the Flood by Noah's age, "in the six hundredth year of Noah's life" (Genesis 7:11).

a: from the first day of the second month until the sixteenth
t: "The first day": not the new moon
p: Ge'ez śärq marks the first day of a month. In Jubilees' calendar it is not tied to the moon.
b: Charles translates śärq as "new moon," and adds in his note on 6:38 that it "could also be translated 'beginnings of the months.'" But Jubilees rejects the moon as a guide (6:36), and its months are fixed blocks of days. So the Plain English Translation says "the first day" of the month, in 6:34 and 6:38 "the start of the month." Genesis gives only one date for going in, "the seventeenth day" of the second month (Genesis 7:11). Jubilees makes the loading last from the first to the sixteenth, and has God close the ark on the seventeenth.

a: with all that we brought to him
p: In Genesis the animals "came to Noah" (Genesis 7:9). In Jubilees the angels bring them.
b: This is a small but telling change. Genesis says the animals "came to Noah, into the ark" (Genesis 7:15). In Jubilees the narrating angels "brought" them. The book often puts angels where Genesis has none, as helpers who carry out God's orders. This goes beyond Genesis without contradicting it.

a: seven windows of the sky
p: Genesis opens "the windows of the sky." Jubilees counts them: seven, and seven mouths of the deep.
b: Genesis 7:11 says "the windows of the sky were opened." Jubilees, which loves the number seven, gives seven windows and seven mouths. Charles compares 1 Enoch 89:2 (in the Animal Apocalypse), where seven channels pour water on the earth. Charles renders mänbäḥbaḥt "flood-gates."

a: Lubar, one of the mountains of Ararat
p: Genesis says "the mountains of Ararat." Jubilees names one peak, Lubar.
b: Genesis 8:4 says "the ark came to rest on the mountains of Ararat," without naming one. Jubilees names the peak Lubar and comes back to it often: Noah plants his vineyard there (7:1), builds his altar there (6:1) and is buried there (10:15). Charles notes that the name also appears in the medieval Hebrew Book of Noah ("in Lubar, of the mountains of Ararat"), and that Epiphanius places Lubar "between the Armenians and the Cardueni."

a: on the seventeenth day of the second month the earth was dry
p: Genesis 8:14 says the twenty-seventh. Jubilees says the seventeenth, then opens the ark on the twenty-seventh.
b: Genesis 8:14 reads: "In the second month, on the twenty-seventh day of the month, the earth was dry." Jubilees has the earth dry on the seventeenth and Noah opening the ark on the twenty-seventh (5:32). Charles reports the argument of B. W. Bacon that the Genesis dates (from the seventeenth of the second month to the twenty-seventh of the second month the next year) add ten days to a lunar year of 354 days, so the Flood lasts exactly one solar year. Jubilees, which counts 364 days, seems to read the Flood the same way (see 6:36, "ten days").

a: On the first day of the third month
p: Noah leaves the ark in the third month, the month of the Feast of Weeks and of Sinai.
b: Genesis gives no date for leaving the ark. Jubilees puts it in the third month, the month in which Israel reached Sinai (Exodus 19:1) and in which Jubilees sets the Feast of Weeks (6:17). Charles notes that the covenant with Abram (14:1) and Jacob's going down to Egypt (44:1) also fall in this month. The book builds a chain of covenants on the same date: Noah, Abraham, Sinai.

a: made atonement with its blood for all the guilt of the earth
p: Genesis has Noah offer burnt offerings. Jubilees adds a sin offering for the earth's guilt.
b: In Genesis 8:20 Noah offers whole burnt offerings of clean animals and birds. Jubilees first has him make atonement "for all the guilt of the earth" with a goat's blood. Charles notes that Jewish tradition outside Jubilees does not know this act, but that the idea fits Numbers 35:33: blood pollutes the land, and "no atonement can be made for the land for the blood shed on it, except by the blood of the one who shed it." Noah's rite goes beyond Genesis by turning him into a priest who follows the laws of Leviticus.

a: an ox, a ram, a sheep, goats, salt, a turtledove and a young dove
p: Genesis has "every clean animal and every clean bird." Jubilees lists the Temple's offerings, with oil, wine, salt and incense.
b: Charles notes that the oil, wine and frankincense are added "in conformity with later ritual" (Exodus 29:40; Leviticus 2:1-2, 13). Salt belongs to every grain offering in Leviticus 2:13. Noah is shown offering the way Israel's priests would offer at the altar. For the writer, the law of sacrifice is not new at Sinai; it was known and kept from the beginning.

a: seedtime and harvest will not stop
p: The promise of Genesis 8:21-22 and the covenant of Genesis 9:11, joined into one.
b: Jubilees joins two promises that Genesis keeps apart: the LORD's words in his heart after smelling the offering (Genesis 8:21-22) and the covenant never again to flood the earth (Genesis 9:11). Here both become one covenant made "with him," with Noah. Genesis' list of seasons is kept: "seedtime and harvest, cold and heat, summer and winter, day and night."

a: Be a blessing
p: Genesis 9:1, 7 say "be fruitful." Jubilees says "be a blessing."
b: Genesis 9:1 has "Be fruitful, grow many, fill the earth." Charles noticed that where Genesis has "grow many," Jubilees has "be a blessing," and discussed how one Hebrew word could have been read as the other. The phrase also recalls God's word to Abram, "And be a blessing!" (Genesis 12:2). The Ge'ez runs: "be for a blessing in the midst of your fear and your dread. I will put (it) on all that is on the earth and in the sea" (ወኩኑ ለበረከት ማእከለ ፍርሃትክሙ ወረዓድክሙ (wäkunu läbäräkät maʾkälä fərhatkəmu wäräʿadkəmu)). The Plain English Translation keeps that order, with the future "I will put." Charles divides it differently: "be a blessing upon it. The fear of you and the dread of you I will inspire in everything," closer to Genesis 9:2, "The fear and terror of you will be on every wild animal of the earth."

a: But flesh with its life, with the blood, you must not eat
p: Genesis 9:4: "Only, flesh with its life, its blood, you must not eat." Jubilees builds a whole law on it.
b: Genesis 9:4-6 is short. Jubilees turns it into the first of its great laws, given to Noah, sworn by his sons (6:10), renewed at Sinai (6:11) and repeated in Noah's last words (7:28-33). Where the Ge'ez says "from the hand of every one," Charles supplied "every beast," from Genesis 9:5 ("From every animal I will demand it"); see the variant. For how Christians read the ban on blood today, see the card on Leviticus 17. "So that your own blood will not be demanded" renders a purpose clause (ከመ ኢይትኃሠሥ ደምክሙ (kämä ʾiytəḫaśäś dämkəmu)).

a: in the image of the Lord he made humankind
p: Murder is answered by death, because humans bear God's image.
b: Jubilees gives Genesis 9:6 almost word for word: whoever spills human blood will have his blood spilled, "for in God's image he made humankind," as the site's Genesis puts it. Ge'ez has no separate word for the divine name, so ʾƎgziʾabḥer here stands where Genesis has Elohim, "God."

a: Noah and his sons swore an oath
t: An oath Genesis does not mention
p: In Genesis God makes the covenant. In Jubilees Noah and his sons also swear to keep it.
b: Genesis 9 is a covenant God makes and keeps on his own. Jubilees adds a human side: Noah and his sons swear not to eat blood, and Noah "made a covenant before the Lord God." This shapes the covenant like the one at Sinai, where the people answered, "Every word the LORD has spoken, we will do" (Exodus 24:3). This goes beyond Genesis.

a: to sprinkle blood on them because of all the words of the covenant
p: The angel ties Noah's covenant to Exodus 24, where Moses splashed blood on the people.
b: Exodus 24:8: "Moses took the blood and splashed it on the people. He said, 'Here is the blood of the covenant that the LORD has cut with you on the terms of all these words.'" Jubilees says that rite repeats Noah's covenant, made in the same month on another mountain. Charles notes that in Noah's covenant blood is something not to eat, while at Sinai it is used to sprinkle and to make atonement (6:14). Jesus' words at the Last Supper, "This is my blood of the covenant" (Mark 14:24), recall the same Exodus scene.

a: This testimony is written for you
p: Ge'ez səmʿ, "testimony": a written witness that binds the people.
b: The word səmʿ ("witness, testimony") runs through Jubilees. A law is a "testimony" because it stands written as a witness: if the people break it, the writing testifies against them. The angel uses the same word of the calendar (6:23, 6:32) and of Noah's charge (7:31).

a: at the hour of morning and of evening
p: Charles: the morning and evening offerings of Numbers 28:3-8.
b: Numbers 28:3-8 commands a lamb in the morning and a lamb at twilight every day. Jubilees links that daily offering with the blood law: the priests' blood on the altar keeps asking forgiveness for Israel. The angel speaks to Moses about the future sanctuary; inside the story no altar of Israel yet exists.

a: He put his bow in the cloud
p: Genesis 9:13: "my bow I have put in the clouds." Jubilees keeps the bow as the covenant's sign.
b: The Ge'ez qäst means a bow, the hunter's or warrior's weapon, as the Hebrew qeshet does. Jubilees does not explain the sign; it simply returns to it after the laws of 6:11-14.

a: the Feast of Weeks
p: Ge'ez bäʿalä subaʿe, the Feast of Weeks of Exodus 34:22. Jubilees never calls it Pentecost.
b: Exodus 34:22: "Hold the Feast of Weeks, with the first crops of the wheat harvest." Charles notes that Jubilees does not use the later name Pentecost ("fiftieth day"), which appears in Tobit 2:1, 2 Maccabees 12:32 and Acts 2:1. Jubilees makes the feast a yearly renewal of the covenant made with Noah.

a: to renew the covenant every year
p: In Jubilees the Feast of Weeks is above all a yearly renewal of the covenant.
b: In Leviticus 23 and Deuteronomy 16 the Feast of Weeks is a harvest feast. Jubilees keeps that side (6:21, "the Feast of Firstfruits") but makes the feast mainly a day for renewing the covenant. The Encyclopaedia Judaica article by Grintz says the book makes Shavuot "commemorate the renewal of the covenant between God and man" after the Flood. Charles notes that later Jewish teaching made the feast the day the law was given at Sinai, an idea he found in Jerome and Augustine but not in Philo or Josephus.

a: This whole feast was kept in heaven
p: Jubilees teaches that the angels kept Israel's feasts in heaven before any human did.
b: This is one of Jubilees' boldest claims, made also of the Sabbath (2:17-18). Charles counts the figures: twenty-six jubilees and five weeks are 1,309 years; seven jubilees and one week are 350, the years Noah lived after the Flood. The feast then lapsed "until the days of Abraham," and the people "ate blood." The 66 books do not say that angels keep Israel's feasts. This goes beyond the Bible. Hebrews 8:5 does speak of the earthly sanctuary as a copy of a heavenly one.

a: But Abraham alone kept it
p: Jubilees later shows Abraham keeping the feast (15:1-2), and Jacob too (44:1-4).
b: This is the chain the angel lays out: Noah, then a lapse, then Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, then forgetting in Egypt, then renewal at Sinai. Charles notes that some of his manuscripts read "But Abraham" and others "And Abraham alone"; VanderKam's text has "alone" (see the variant). The book tells of Abraham's feast in 15:1-2.

a: This feast is double and of two kinds
p: The Feast of Weeks is two feasts at once: the covenant feast and the firstfruits feast.
b: Ge'ez kəlʾe ʿəḍfät, "double," and kəlʾe zämäd, "two kinds." The angel explains: it is "the Feast of Weeks" and "the Feast of Firstfruits." The Bible gives the feast both names: Exodus 23:16 calls it the Feast of Harvest "for the first crops of your work," Numbers 28:26 "the day of the firstfruits." Jubilees makes the two names two sides of one day: a harvest and an oath.
orig: ክልኤ ዕፅፈት ይእቲ ወለክልኤ ዘመድ (kəlʾe ʿəḍfät yəʾti wäläkləʾe zämäd)

a: the book of the first law
p: The angel says he wrote of the feast "in the book of the first law." Most take that to mean the Torah.
b: The angel of the presence claims to have written the feast "in the book of the first law," and so the Plain English Translation keeps "first." The phrase seems to mean the books of Moses (here, Leviticus 23 and Numbers 28), with Jubilees as a second, fuller account. Readers who receive Jubilees as Scripture take it as the angel's own claim of agreement with the Torah. It can also be read as the writer presenting his book as a companion to the Pentateuch, not a rival. Compare 1:26-29, where the angel is told to write.

a: days of remembrance and days of the seasons
p: The first days of months 1, 4, 7 and 10 open the four quarters of Jubilees' year.
b: Jubilees divides the year into four quarters of thirteen weeks (6:29). The first day of each quarter is a feast "of remembrance." Grintz, in the Encyclopaedia Judaica, calls them the book's "four new years" and notes that the rabbis too knew four new years (Mishnah Rosh Hashanah 1:1), though with other dates and meanings. Jubilees ties each day to a moment of the Flood (6:25-27). Charles lists other events the book places on these days, such as Adam and Eve leaving Eden on the first of the fourth month (3:32).

a: so that through them they became a memorial for him
p: The four days keep Noah's memory alive: each marks a step of the Flood.
b: Ge'ez täzkar, "memorial, remembrance," the same word as the "days of remembrance" in 6:23. The feasts are not only fixed points of the year but reminders of what God did for Noah, as the Passover reminds Israel of the Exodus (Exodus 12:14).

a: On the first day of the first month he was told to make himself the ark
t: The four days in the Flood
p: Each of the four days marks a step: the ark ordered and the earth dry, the deep shut, the deep opened, the mountains seen.
b: The four days match the dates of 5:29-30 and Genesis 8. The first of the first month: the order to build (as Charles notes, also 5:21) and the dry earth (Genesis 8:13). The first of the fourth: the deep shut (5:29). The first of the seventh: the deep opened to drain (5:29). The first of the tenth: the mountain tops seen (Genesis 8:5). So the calendar is presented as written into the Flood itself.

a: Thirteen weeks lie between each of them and the next
p: Four quarters of thirteen weeks make 52 weeks, 364 days.
b: Charles reads verses 29-30 as a year of four seasons, each of three months or thirteen weeks. Grintz describes the year as exactly 52 weeks, with months of 30 days except the third, sixth, ninth and twelfth, which have 31. Thirteen weeks are 91 days: 30 + 30 + 31. Four quarters of 91 days make 364. Because 364 divides by seven, every date falls on the same day of the week every year.

a: This is how it is engraved and decreed on the heavenly tablets
p: Charles's English puts this sentence at the end of 6:30. VanderKam's Ge'ez starts 6:31 with it.
b: Charles (1913) ends verse 30 with "Thus it is engraven and ordained on the heavenly tablets." In VanderKam's Ge'ez the sentence opens verse 31. The words are the same; only the verse break differs. The Plain English Translation follows VanderKam's numbering.

a: 364 days
p: Jubilees, like 1 Enoch's Astronomical Book, commands a year of exactly 364 days.
b: 1 Enoch 82:6 says, "The year is complete in 364 days," and 1 Enoch 72:32, "The year comes to exactly 364 days." Jubilees makes that count a law given to Moses. Its own verses fix only the quarters of thirteen weeks (6:29) and the fifty-two weeks (6:30); they do not say how long each month is (see the chapter page for Grintz's and Charles's views). The true solar year is about 365 and a quarter days, so a 364-day calendar falls behind the seasons unless days are added. Charles thought the writers knew Greek calendars and chose 364 days anyway, out of "dogmatic prejudice" in his words, so that every feast would fall on the same weekday. The Bible itself commands no fixed number of days for the year. This goes beyond the 66 books. For how churches answer the question, see the card at 1 Enoch 82, "Must God's people keep a set calendar of holy days?"

a: They will upset the times, the years will be shifted
p: The Ge'ez says twice that the times will be upset and the years shifted.
b: The second half of the verse repeats the first almost word for word. Charles put the repeat in brackets as a copying slip. The Plain English Translation keeps it, since VanderKam's text has it, and since the repeat may also be the speaker's emphasis.

a: the division of the days
p: Ge'ez kufale, "division": the Ethiopian name of the whole book.
b: Here the Ge'ez word is kufalehu lämäwaʿl, "its division of the days." Kufale, "Division," is the name of Jubilees in the Ethiopian Bible, from the book's own words about "the divisions of the times" (1:4, 1:29). The book claims that the true division of time is not human work: "it is not from my own heart," the angel says, echoing Moses' words in Numbers 16:28.

a: walk in the feasts of the nations
p: Losing the calendar means keeping holy days by the nations' count, not God's.
b: For Jubilees, keeping the wrong calendar is not a small error. It means living by "the feasts of the nations." The writer does not say whom he means, and Charles's English says only "the Gentiles." Charles also notes that the Samaritan Chronicle, which knew Jubilees, argued against reckoning by the sun alone. The next verse names one fault of the wrong count: it follows the moon (6:36).

a: there will be people who watch the moon closely
p: Jubilees says the moon "ruins the seasons." Genesis 1:14 gave sun and moon both for seasons.
b: Genesis 1:14 says God made the lights in the sky, the sun and the moon: "They will be signs, and will mark the appointed times, the days and the years." Jubilees 2:9 gives the sun alone that task. Here the angel warns against people who set the months by watching the moon. A lunar year is 354 days, Charles notes, ten days short of 364: hence "ten days early" each year. The site's 1 Enoch counts the same 364-day year (1 Enoch 74:12; 1 Enoch 82:6) but also describes the moon's course at length (1 Enoch 73-74) and says, "The moon brings in the years for them exactly." Charles therefore wrote that Jubilees "seems to be a polemic against the teaching of Ethiopic Enoch lxxiii.-lxxiv." That is his theory: the two books agree on 364 days and differ on whether the moon has any part in the count. This conflicts with the plain sense of Genesis 1:14 and Psalm 104:19 ("He made the moon to keep the appointed times"). For how churches answer the question, see the card at 1 Enoch 82.

a: the holy with the unclean
p: Keeping a feast on the wrong day makes a holy day common and a common day holy.
b: This is the reason the calendar matters so much to the writer. If the count is wrong, people will work on a holy day and feast on an ordinary one. The language echoes the priests' duty in Leviticus 10:10: "You must separate the holy from the ordinary, and the unclean from the clean."

a: they will eat every kind of blood with every kind of flesh
p: The chapter ends by tying its two laws together: the right year and no blood.
b: Chapter 6 began with the blood law and ends with it. For the writer the two go together: a people who keep God's time also keep God's food laws, and a people who lose one lose the other. The same pairing ran through 6:18, where Noah's sons "ruined" the feast "and they ate blood."

a: They bore fruit in the fourth year
t: Noah keeps the law of fruit trees
p: Noah waits until the fourth year and holds his feast in the fifth, as Leviticus 19:23-25 commands.
b: Genesis 9:20 says only that Noah "was the first to plant a vineyard." Jubilees has him keep the law of Leviticus 19:23-25: "In the fourth year all its fruit will be holy, a gift of praise to the LORD. In the fifth year you may eat its fruit." Charles notes that the verse is meant to call that law to mind. Noah picks the fourth-year fruit, keeps the wine, and drinks only in the fifth year (7:2). He spells out the law in 7:35-37. This goes beyond Genesis.

a: until the first day, the first day of the first month
p: Noah opens the wine on the first day of the first month, one of his four remembrance days.
b: The first of the first month is one of the four days Noah decreed (6:23). So the feast of 7:3 is a New Year feast, held on a day the book has just made holy. Charles notes that the book puts other first-month events on the same day.

a: one young bull from the herd, one ram, seven sheep a year old, and one young goat
p: Charles: the list follows the offerings for the first day of the seventh month in Numbers 29.
b: Charles says the ritual follows mainly Numbers 29:2, 5: one young bull, one ram, seven yearling lambs, and a male goat as a sin offering. That list belongs to the first day of the seventh month. Jubilees uses it for Noah's New Year sacrifice. The goat comes first (7:4), as the sin offering, "to make atonement."

a: He was drunk
p: Genesis says Noah "became drunk." Jubilees keeps it, but after a holy feast and a full offering.
b: Genesis 9:21 says Noah "drank some of the wine, became drunk, and uncovered himself in the middle of his tent." Jubilees keeps all of it. But by setting it after a priestly sacrifice and a feast "with joy," shared with his children, it makes Noah's drinking part of a festival, not careless excess. Jubilees does not blame Noah at all and puts the blame on Ham.

a: they covered their father's nakedness
p: Ge'ez ḫafrät, which Charles renders "shame" in 7:20: what must be covered.
b: Genesis 9:23 uses ʿerwah, "nakedness." The Ge'ez has ḫafrät, which Charles renders "shame" in 7:20, the same word as in 7:20, where Noah tells his grandsons "to cover the nakedness of their flesh," and as in 3:31, where Jubilees says Israel must cover its nakedness, unlike the nations. Covering nakedness is a law of the heavenly tablets in Jubilees.

a: An owned slave he will be to his brothers
p: The Hebrew says "a slave of slaves." The Ge'ez says "a slave who is owned," like the Greek.
b: Genesis 9:25 says Canaan will be "a slave of slaves" (Hebrew ʿeved ʿavadim). The Ge'ez has qənuyä gäbrä, "an owned slave," a slave acquired as property. Charles notes that the Septuagint has pais oiketēs, "a household slave," and Onkelos a similar phrase. So Jubilees agrees with the Greek here. The curse falls on Canaan, not on Ham, as in Genesis; it was never a curse on Africa or on dark skin, a misuse that the text itself does not support.
orig: ቅኑየ ገብረ ይኩን ለአኃዊሁ (qənuyä gäbrä yəkun läʾäḫawihu)

a: his younger son
p: Genesis 9:24 calls him "his youngest son." The Ge'ez says "his son who is small," which can mean younger or youngest.
b: Ge'ez wäldu zäynəʾs, "his son who is small." The Ge'ez form does not mark "younger" against "youngest," so the English has to choose; the Plain English Translation says "younger." In 4:33 Jubilees gives the birth order Shem, Ham, Japheth, which would make Ham younger than Shem but not the youngest. Charles notes that Jubilees treats Shem as the eldest (10:14), reading Genesis 10:21 as "the older brother of Japheth," as the site's Genesis also does. Either way, which son is meant is an inference from the order of the names.

a: may the Lord live in the dwelling of Shem
t: Who will live in Shem's tents?
p: In Genesis 9:27 "he" is unclear: God or Japheth? Jubilees says plainly: the Lord.
b: Genesis 9:27 reads "May God make room for Japheth, and may he live in the tents of Shem." The Hebrew does not say who "he" is. Jubilees supplies "the Lord," so the blessing means God will dwell with Shem's line, which Jubilees later ties to Zion and the Temple (8:18-19). Charles notes that Onkelos reads it the same way (God's presence resting in Shem's dwellings), while Targum Pseudo-Jonathan and Justin Martyr take "he" to be Japheth.

a: Let Canaan be their slave
p: Genesis 9:27 says "his slave." The Ge'ez says "their slave," of Shem and Japheth both.
b: Ge'ez gäbromu, "their servant." The plural takes in both brothers blessed in verses 11-12. It may also reflect the book's interest in Canaan's guilt, which grows in 10:29-34.

a: Ham knew that his father had cursed his younger son
p: Jubilees adds why the family split: Ham resented the curse on his son.
b: Genesis never says how Ham took the curse. Jubilees makes him angry and has him leave his father, with his sons. "His younger son" here is Ham's own youngest, Canaan, the last in the list of Genesis 10:6. The split begins the rivalry between the brothers that leads to Japheth's jealousy (7:15) and to Noah's warnings (7:26).

a: Neelatamauk
p: Jubilees names the three sons' wives and their cities. Genesis gives none of these names.
b: Charles notes that the Syriac list of patriarchs' wives (a list "according to the Hebrew book called Jubilees") has the same three names. He suggests Hebrew roots: Neelatamauk perhaps from naḥalah, "inheritance"; Sedeqatelbab from tsidqat lev, "righteousness of heart" (7:16). Each brother names his city after his wife, and the righteous name goes to Shem.

a: But Shem stayed with his father Noah
p: Shem builds beside his father on the mountain; the others leave.
b: Charles notes that the detail is there to show Shem's love for his father. The sons who separate (Ham) or envy (Japheth) are set against the son who stays. It prepares for Shem receiving Noah's books (10:14) and the best portion of the earth (8:12-21).

a: Aram and Lud
p: Genesis 10:22 lists Elam, Asshur, Arpachshad, Lud and Aram. The Ge'ez order and wording here are uncertain.
b: The letters in VanderKam's Ge'ez (ʾäram wəlud) can be read "Aram and Lud" or "Aram, children." Charles says he emended the verse and prints Lud before Aram, as in Genesis 10:22. The aside about Arpachshad, born "two years after the flood," comes from Genesis 11:10. See the variant.

a: Noah began to command his grandsons
p: Noah gives his grandsons a short code of law, long before Sinai.
b: Noah's list here: do what is right, cover nakedness, bless the Creator, honor father and mother, love one another, and keep away from sexual sin, uncleanness and all wrongdoing. Then come the bans on bloodshed and eating blood (7:28-33) and the fruit-tree law (7:35-37). Charles thought verses 20-39 come from an older "Book of Noah," because Noah speaks in the first person from 7:26 on.

a: sexual sin
p: Ge'ez zəmut covers sexual sin of every kind; 7:21 uses it of the Watchers.
b: The noun zəmut and its verb (7:21) cover sexual wrongdoing in general: prostitution, adultery, forbidden unions. The Plain English Translation uses "sexual sin," the wording the site uses for porneia in Acts 15:20.

a: these three things
p: Sexual sin, uncleanness and wrongdoing (7:20): the three sins that brought the Flood.
b: Charles takes "these three things" to be the three sins named at the end of 7:20: sexual sin, uncleanness and all wrongdoing. He compares Genesis Rabbah 31, which gives idolatry, sexual sin and bloodshed as the Flood's causes, and the Talmud's teaching (Sanhedrin 74a) that these three are the sins one must die rather than commit. In Jubilees the three are told as one story: the Watchers' sexual sin, the uncleanness it began, and the bloodshed of the giants (7:22-25).

a: the Watchers
p: Ge'ez təguhan, "those who stay awake": the angels of 4:15 and 5:1. Here, for the first time in this part, they are called by this name.
b: The Watchers (Aramaic ʿirin, Greek egrēgoroi) are the angels of 1 Enoch 6-16. The Aramaic word appears in the Bible only in Daniel 4:13, 17 and 23, "a watcher, a holy one." In 5:1 Jubilees called them "the angels of the Lord"; here, for the first time in this part, Noah uses the name. "Against the command of their judgments" (እምትእዛዘ ኵነኔሆሙ (ʾəmtəʾzazä kʷənänehomu); the noun is the one rendered "judgment" in 5:13-14 and 10:6, where Charles has "the law of their ordinances"): in Jubilees they were sent to teach and do justice (4:15), and broke the law of their own nature by going after women.

a: the Naphidim
p: Ge'ez nafidim: the Nephilim of Genesis 6:4. Jubilees, like 1 Enoch, knows three kinds of giants.
b: Genesis 6:4 says "the Nephilim were on the earth." The Ge'ez nafidim is the same word, slightly changed in copying. Charles explains the verse from the Greek of 1 Enoch 7:1-2 in Syncellus, where the women bore "great giants," the giants bore the Nephilim, and the Nephilim bore the Eliud. Charles's English of Jubilees has the same three steps: "the Giants," the Naphil and the Eljo. Where Charles has "the Giants," VanderKam's Ge'ez has an unclear word, yarbəḥ, so in the Plain English Translation the sentence names four (see the note and variant on "Yarbeh"). Each kills the next, then humans kill one another.

a: none of them were alike
p: The Ge'ez says the giants were "not alike." Charles thought the word was corrupt.
b: Ge'ez ʾiytəmasälu, "they do not resemble one another." Charles suspected a copying error and suggested a word meaning "they plundered one another" or "they fought one another" (as in 1 Enoch 15:11). The Plain English Translation keeps the Ge'ez. "Not alike" may simply mean the three kinds of giants were different from one another.

a: Yarbeh
p: Ge'ez yarbəḥ is unclear. Charles's English has "the Giants," the first of the three kinds.
b: The Ge'ez word yarbəḥ is not a common word, and in this sentence it stands where a name or a class of giants is needed. Charles's English has "the Giants," the first kind in the Greek of 1 Enoch 7 (see the note on "the Naphidim"); his note does not discuss the word. The Plain English Translation keeps VanderKam's form as a name, so the verse names four where Charles has three kinds. See the variant.

a: Every one sold himself to do wrong
p: The phrase is used of Ahab in 1 Kings 21:20 and 25.
b: Charles points to 1 Kings 21:20, where Elijah tells Ahab "you sold yourself to do what the LORD sees as evil." The picture is of a person handing himself over to evil like a slave sold to a master. "The earth was filled with wrongdoing" recalls Genesis 6:11.

a: After these came all the others
t: A short verse in the Ge'ez
p: The Ge'ez lacks a verb here. Charles supplied "they sinned against" from 1 Enoch 7:5.
b: Word for word the Ge'ez says: "And after these, all of them: wild animals and birds and what moves and what walks on the earth." Charles added "they sinned against" from 1 Enoch 7:5, where the giants "began to sin against birds, animals, creeping things and fish." Without the addition, the verse says the animals followed the humans into bloodshed, as in 5:2. The Plain English Translation keeps the Ge'ez and fills in only "came."

a: We were left, I and you, my children
t: Noah speaks in the first person
p: From here to 7:39 Noah speaks as "I." Charles thought the speech was taken from an older Book of Noah.
b: Verse 20 tells about Noah's teaching; from verse 26 Noah suddenly speaks for himself. Charles took the change as a sign that the writer copied a "Book of Noah" without adapting it, and thought 10:1-14 came from the same work. Others think the writer simply moved from report to speech, as Genesis 49 or Deuteronomy do. Whether such a Book of Noah ever existed is debated.

a: the demons have begun to lead you and your children astray
p: Noah fears that demons are already at work in his family. Chapter 10 tells what he did.
b: Ge'ez ʾägannət, "demons." In 10:5 they are called the children of the Watchers, "these spirits." The 66 books never say where demons come from; Jubilees, like 1 Enoch 15:8-9, says they are the spirits of the dead giants. This goes beyond the Bible. For the church debate, see the card on 1 Enoch 15.

a: they will go into Sheol, they will go down into the place of judgment
t: Sheol and the place of judgment
p: Charles prints this as poetry and thinks 1 Enoch 103:7-8 borrowed from it.
b: The verse falls into short parallel lines in the Ge'ez, which Charles prints as verse. He compares 1 Enoch 103:7-8, where the souls of sinners go down "into Sheol" and "darkness." "The place of judgment" (mäkanä däyn) is the same place where the spirits are bound in 10:5, 9 and 11.
orig: ውስተ ሲኦል የሐውሩ ወውስተ መካን ዘደይን ይወርዱ (wəstä siʾol yäḥäwru wäwsətä mäkan zädäyn yəwärdu)

a: by covering what is spilled on the face of the earth
p: Ge'ez dafana means "cover." Charles warns against "bury."
b: Leviticus 17:13 commands a hunter to pour out the blood of an animal he catches and "cover it with earth." Charles stresses that the Ge'ez dafana means "cover," not "bury," and that one older scholar built a whole argument for Christian authorship on the wrong rendering "burying." "Do a good work for yourselves" uses məṣwat, a word for a good deed or alms.

a: by the blood of the one who spilled it the earth will be made clean
p: Only the killer's death can cleanse the land of bloodshed.
b: Numbers 35:33: "No atonement can be made for the land for the blood shed on it, except by the blood of the one who shed it." Noah teaches that law to his grandsons. It is also why the Flood had to come: the earth was soaked with blood (7:25) and could be cleansed only by the death of those who spilled it.

a: so that you may be planted in righteousness
p: Israel as a plant set in the earth is a favorite image of Jubilees and 1 Enoch.
b: Charles lists Jeremiah 11:17 and Amos 9:15 for the image of God planting his people, and 1 Enoch 10:16 and 93:5, 10, where Israel is "the plant of righteousness." Jubilees uses the same picture in 1:16 and 16:26.

a: who saved me from the waters of the flood
p: Charles thought 2 Peter 2:5 knew this speech of Noah.
b: 2 Peter 2:5 says God "guarded Noah, the eighth one, a herald of righteousness, when he brought a flood on a world of ungodly people." Genesis never shows Noah preaching. Charles noted that here Noah does preach righteousness, speaks of being saved from the Flood, and calls Enoch "the seventh" (7:39), and he concluded that the writer of 2 Peter knew this passage. Others think 2 Peter draws on a wider tradition of Noah as a preacher.

a: the servants of the Lord's house are to eat before the altar
p: Jubilees gives the leftover fourth-year fruit to the priests. Later rabbis gave it to the owner.
b: Leviticus 19:24 says the fourth-year fruit is "holy, a gift of praise to the LORD," but not who eats it. Charles explains that Jubilees has the first fruits offered on the altar and the rest eaten by "the servants of the Lord's house," the priests. He notes that later Jewish law took the other view: the fruit belonged to its owners, to be eaten in Jerusalem (Josephus, Antiquities 4.8.19), and the Sifre on Numbers denies the priests a share. The Plain English Translation follows the Ge'ez; Charles's English adds "and all things" after "heaven and earth," which VanderKam's Ge'ez does not have.

a: In the fifth year make its release
p: Ge'ez ḫədgät, "release": the fruit is set free for ordinary use.
b: The word means "letting go, release," the same family of words used for the seventh-year release of debts in Deuteronomy 15. In the fifth year the fruit is "released" from its holy status, and the owner may eat it, as Leviticus 19:25 says.

a: the seventh in his generation
p: Jude 14 also calls Enoch "the seventh from Adam."
b: Jude 14: "Enoch, the seventh from Adam, also prophesied about these people." 1 Enoch 60:8 and 93:3 say the same. Counting Adam as the first, Enoch is seventh in the line of Genesis 5. Noah says the laws he teaches came down from Enoch through Methuselah and Lamech (7:38). Charles notes that the writer credits Enoch with laws, not only with visions.

a: Kainam
p: Hebrew Genesis has no Kainam between Arpachshad and Shelah. The Greek Genesis and Luke 3:36 do.
b: In the Hebrew of Genesis 11:12, Arpachshad is the father of Shelah. Charles notes that the Septuagint of Genesis 11:13 and Luke 3:36 add a generation, Cainan: "the son of Cainan, the son of Arphaxad." Jubilees has the same extra name. Charles thought the name was added so that there would be twenty-two heads of humankind from Adam to Jacob, matching the twenty-two works of creation (2:23). Ge'ez qaynam.

a: Rasueja, daughter of Susan, daughter of Elam
p: Jubilees names the wife of every patriarch, often a close cousin. Genesis does not.
b: Charles derives Rasueja from Hebrew retsuyah, "the accepted one" (compare Deuteronomy 33:24), and notes that the Syriac list of wives has the name. He also brackets "daughter of Susan" as an addition, since a woman named for a son's granddaughter is odd. Susan is a person here; the city Susa in 8:21 has the same letters in Ge'ez.

a: the teaching of the Watchers
p: Kainam finds the Watchers' star-lore cut in stone, copies it, and goes astray.
b: Jubilees says the Watchers taught people to read omens in the sun, moon and stars. This links with 1 Enoch 8:3, where Watchers teach the signs of the earth, the stars and the moon. The Bible forbids reading omens (Deuteronomy 18:10-12) and mocks the star-gazers of Babylon (Isaiah 47:13). Charles traces the story in later writers: Josephus credits the knowledge of the stars to Seth's children, written on two pillars, and Syncellus says Kainam "found the writing of the giants" and hid it. Here the knowledge is not from Seth but from the Watchers, and so it is sin.

a: went astray because of it
p: Ge'ez räsʿä can mean "forget" or "act wickedly." Cedrenus's Greek has "he sinned in them."
b: The verb räsʿä is from the same root as räsiʿ, "ungodly," and as "forget" (6:19 "forgot"). Charles translates "sinned owing to it," and notes that the Greek chronicler Cedrenus keeps the same idea: "he sinned in them, and taught others the same."

a: Shelah, for he said, "I have truly been sent."
p: The name Shelah sounds like Hebrew shalaḥ, "send." The pun works only in Hebrew.
b: Charles points out the play on words in the Hebrew behind the Ge'ez: "he called his name Shelah, for he said, I have been sent (shullaḥti)." The Ge'ez spells the name Sala, like the Greek Sala, but keeps the explanation. Such puns are one sign that Jubilees was written in Hebrew.

a: Azurad, daughter of Nebrod
p: Charles thought Azurad should be Azura, as in the Syriac list. Nebrod looks like a form of Nimrod.
b: Charles says the name should be read Azura, as in the Syriac list of wives and a Greek manuscript of Genesis that he cites. Nebrod looks like a form of Nimrod (Genesis 10:8); if so, Jubilees has Eber marry Nimrod's daughter, which Genesis does not say.

a: That is why he named him Peleg
t: Peleg and the dividing of the earth
p: Genesis 10:25: "for in his days the earth was split up." Jubilees explains how.
b: The name Peleg sounds like the Hebrew verb palag, "divide." Genesis 10:25 says Eber named his son Peleg "for in his days the earth was split up," without saying more. Jubilees tells two divisions: a first one done "in a wicked way" by Noah's descendants (8:9), and a proper one by lot under Noah and an angel (8:10-9:15).

a: in a wicked way
p: Charles saw the secret division set against a lawful one under Noah.
b: Charles calls this "secret and unauthoritative division" a foil for the formal one that follows, made by Noah "in the presence of an angel," and sworn to with an oath (9:14-15). He compares Pirke de-Rabbi Eliezer 24, a later midrash that also tells of the division of the earth.

a: one of us who had been sent
t: An angel present at the lots
p: One of the angels of the presence watches over the division. In 10:32 he is "the holy judge."
b: Charles takes this angel to be one of the angels of the presence, the ones God sent to bind the Watchers (5:6). His presence makes the lots God's choice and not a human deal. In 10:32 Canaan's brothers remind him of the oath sworn "before the holy judge."

a: took the writing from the bosom of their father Noah
p: The sons draw written lots from the fold of Noah's robe.
b: The "bosom" is the fold of a robe at the chest, where things were carried. Lots could be drawn from such a fold: "People throw the lot into the lap" (Proverbs 16:33). Epiphanius, quoted by Charles, says Noah divided the world among his three sons "by casting lots" at Rhinocorura, on the border of Egypt and Palestine.

a: the middle of the earth
p: Shem's lot is the center of the world, where the holy places lie (8:19).
b: Ezekiel 38:12 describes Israel as a people who "live at the center of the earth" (Hebrew "the navel of the earth"), and in Ezekiel 5:5 God says of Jerusalem, "I put her in the middle of the nations." Charles notes that the rabbis kept the idea: the land of Israel is the navel of the world, and Jerusalem is in its middle. In Jubilees Shem's portion is the middle band of the world, between Japheth's cold north and Ham's hot south (8:30).

a: the Tina River
p: Charles: the Tina is the Don, the Rafa mountains the Rhipaean range, and Me'at the Sea of Azov.
b: Jubilees draws its world map in the terms of Greek geography. Charles identifies the Tina with the Tanais, the river Don; the Rafa mountains with the Rhipaean mountains, which ancient writers placed far to the north; the sea of Me'at with Lake Maeotis, the Sea of Azov; and the Great Sea with the Mediterranean. The writer's world is the round earth of the Greek maps, divided among the sons of Noah.

a: the tongue that faces south
p: Ge'ez ləsan, "tongue," can mean a cape of land or a bay of the sea.
b: Charles notes that ləsan may mean either a promontory or a gulf. The Bible uses the same picture: Isaiah 11:15 speaks of "the tongue of Egypt's sea," and Joshua 15:2, 5 of the "tongues" of the Dead Sea. In 8:14 "the Tongue of the Egyptian Sea" is, Charles thinks, the Gulf of Aqaba or the gulfs of the Red Sea.

a: the Gihon River
p: The Gihon, one of Eden's rivers, is the Nile here, the border of Ham's land.
b: Genesis 2:13 says of the Gihon, "It circles the whole land of Cush." Charles notes that Jubilees identifies the Gihon with the Nile, as Syncellus later did ("the Nile, which is also called Gihon"), and as the Greek of Sirach 24:27 does. Afra, Charles suggests, is Africa in its early, narrow sense.

a: the Garden of Eden
p: Jubilees puts Eden in the east, inside Shem's portion.
b: Genesis 2:8 says God planted a garden "in Eden, toward the east." Jubilees follows it and makes Eden part of Shem's lot. The verse has a doubled phrase, "on the south side of it, to the south" (መንገለ ሰሜኑ ለሰሜን (mängälä sämenu läsämen)). Charles brackets the second "to the south" as a dittography, a phrase copied twice by mistake, and notes on "south" here, "Better translate 'north.'" The Plain English Translation keeps the Ge'ez as it stands. See the variant.

a: the Garden of Eden is the Holy of Holies
p: Eden, Sinai and Zion: the three holy places of Shem's land, facing one another.
b: Jubilees treats Eden as the first sanctuary, the true Holy of Holies, which is why Adam and Eve could not enter it until purified (3:9-14). Sinai is "the center of the desert," and Zion "the center of the navel of the earth." In 4:26 the book named four holy places, adding the Mount of the East; Charles wondered whether that fourth was Lubar, in Japheth's land. Ezekiel 28:13-14 also sets Eden beside "the holy mountain of God": "You were on the holy mountain of God."

a: He blessed the God of gods
p: Deuteronomy 10:17 and Psalm 136:2 call the LORD "God of gods."
b: Ge'ez ʾAmlakä ʾamalkət, "God of gods." The title is biblical: "the LORD your God is the God of gods and the Lord of lords" (Deuteronomy 10:17). Noah praises God because the lots fell as his own prophecy had said (8:18; 7:11-12).

a: the whole land of Bashan
p: Some names are biblical (Bashan, Lebanon, Senir, Amana, Caphtor); others are hard to place.
b: The Ge'ez spells Bashan Basa, Senir Sanir and Caphtor Kaftur; the Plain English Translation uses the Bible's forms. Charles notes that Senir is the Amorite name for Hermon (Deuteronomy 3:9), and that Senir and Amana appear together in Song of Songs 4:8. On "the islands of Caphtor," he weighs Cappadocia (as many ancient versions took Caphtor) against Crete. "India" is ʾIndäke; the Red Sea is ʾErtəra, the Greek "Erythraean Sea."
r: Deuteronomy 3:9; Song of Songs 4:8; Amos 9:7; Jeremiah 47:4

a: the sea into which everything goes down that is not destroyed
p: Charles thought the text was damaged: perhaps "anything that goes into it perishes."
b: The sea of Ma'uk lies at the far west. Charles wondered whether the name was a garbled form of Ōkeanos, the Ocean stream around the world, and thought the description had probably lost its sense in copying: "if anything descends into it, it perishes." The sea of Atel is, he suggests, the Atlantic; Gadir (8:23) is Gades, modern Cadiz in Spain.

a: a mix of cold and heat
p: Japheth's land is cold, Ham's hot, and Shem's just right.
b: The last line praises Shem's portion: neither too hot nor too cold. Jubilees claims the blessing for Shem's line, and so for Israel: the land God gives is the best and most balanced on earth, as Deuteronomy 8:7-10 describes "a good land."

a: The first portion came out for Cush, toward the east
p: Ham's four sons are placed east to west: Cush, Mizraim, Put, Canaan.
b: Genesis 10:6 lists "Cush, Mizraim, Put and Canaan." Jubilees turns the list into a map running from east to west, with Canaan at the far west by the sea. This matters for 10:29: Canaan's lot was in the far west, by the sea, not in the land later called Canaan. Charles took it to be north-west Africa.

a: The first portion came out for Elam and his sons
p: Shem's five sons of Genesis 10:22 get lands from east to west.
b: Genesis 10:22 lists Shem's sons: "Elam, Asshur, Arpachshad, Lud and Aram." Jubilees gives each a land: Elam the far east toward India; Asshur Assyria and Shinar (9:3); Arpachshad the land of the Chaldeans and Lebanon (9:4); Aram Mesopotamia (9:5); Lud the mountains of Asshur toward the Great Sea (9:6). Charles's 1913 English has "for Ham" in this verse where the Ge'ez plainly reads Elam (läʾelam).

a: Sak
p: Ge'ez wäsäk and wädäfa are unclear. Charles emended the second to "and skirts the river."
b: The Ge'ez lists "Asshur, Nineveh, Shinar and Sak." Charles leaves Sak out of his English. The verse ends with wädäfa fäläg, which Charles calls untranslatable as it stands. He emended it to "and skirts the river," and noted that if Wadafa were a river's name, it could be read "to the river Wadafa." The Plain English Translation takes both as names, since neither can be checked; no river of that name appears anywhere else in the book. See the variant.

a: the region of the Chaldeans
p: Josephus also linked Arpachshad with the Chaldeans.
b: Charles notes that Josephus (Antiquities 1.6.4) makes Arpachshad the ancestor of the Chaldeans. Abram's home is "Ur of the Chaldeans" (Genesis 11:28), so Jubilees puts Abram's ancestor in the right land. The lot also includes Lebanon, Senir and Amana, the northern edge of the promised land.

a: Madai's portion came out for him to hold
p: Charles: Madai's lot seems to be the far northwest of Europe; in 10:35 he leaves it.
b: Madai is the ancestor of the Medes (Genesis 10:2). Charles thought his lot here covered the far northwest of Europe, perhaps Britain and Ireland, and noted that later chronicles name Britain among Japheth's lands. In 10:35 Madai dislikes his portion and asks his wife's brothers for land in the east, which is how Jubilees explains why the Medes lived among Shem's peoples.

a: For Javan the fourth portion came out
p: Javan is Ionia, the Greeks. Their lot is the islands.
b: Javan is the Hebrew name for the Ionians, the Greeks of the Aegean coast (Isaiah 66:19; Ezekiel 27:13), and in Daniel 8:21 the Greek kingdom. Charles notes that here Javan holds the islands near Asia Minor. For a writer in Judea under Greek rule, giving the Greeks only islands is a pointed choice.

a: The islands of Kamaturi fell by lot to the sons of Arpachshad
p: Charles bracketed this sentence: Arpachshad is Shem's son, but the verse is about Japheth's.
b: Charles thought this sentence did not belong here, because 9:7-13 deals with Japheth's sons, and Arpachshad is a son of Shem. He suggested it once followed 9:4, and that Kamaturi may be a garbled form of Kaftur, Caphtor (8:21). The Plain English Translation keeps it where VanderKam's text has it.

a: He made them all swear an oath with a curse
p: Charles: the oath explains why Israel later had a right to the land of Canaan.
b: Charles saw in this oath the key to chapters 8-10. If Noah's sons swore, under a curse, never to take another's lot, then Canaan broke the oath when he settled in Shem's land (10:29-34). Israel, Shem's descendant, would then be taking back its own land, not seizing someone else's. Charles thought the writer was answering moral objections, current in his day, to Israel's conquest of Canaan. He quotes Epiphanius making the same argument: "they have received back their own land which had been plundered from them." See the chapter page.

a: So be it! So be it!
p: The double answer recalls Israel's "Amen" to the curses of Deuteronomy 27.
b: The Ge'ez läykun wäläykun, "let it be, let it be," is the Ethiopic way of saying "Amen, amen." In Deuteronomy 27:15-26 all the people answer each curse with "Amen." Here Noah's descendants take the curse on themselves and on their children until the day of judgment.

a: the unclean demons
p: Charles: the spirits of the giants, the children of the Watchers.
b: Ge'ez ʾägannət rəkusan, "unclean demons." Charles explains them as the spirits that went out of the giants, with 1 Enoch 15-16. He also reports the medieval Hebrew Book of Noah, which has a close parallel to this verse: "the spirits of the bastards began to stir" against Noah's sons, "to lead astray, to make err, to destroy and to strike." The Gospels' "unclean spirits" (Mark 1:23) are a related idea.

a: God of the spirits that are in all flesh
p: Numbers 16:22: "God, God of the spirits of all flesh."
b: Moses and Aaron pray with this title in Numbers 16:22 and 27:16. Noah uses it as he asks God to rule the evil spirits: the God who gives every living being its spirit is the only one with power over spirits (10:6). Ge'ez ʾAmlakä mänafəst; compare 1 Enoch's "Lord of Spirits."

a: the children of ruin
p: Ge'ez wəludä ḥägul, "children of destruction," the giants destroyed before the Flood.
b: Charles compares 2 Thessalonians 2:3, where the man of lawlessness is "the son of ruin." Here the phrase names the generation destroyed in the Flood, or the giants themselves. Noah thanks God that he was not treated like them.

a: over the children of your children
p: Noah calls his grandsons God's children. Charles's text has "my sons."
b: VanderKam's Ge'ez reads wəludä wəludkä, "the children of your children," addressing God. Noah speaks of his family as God's own children. One of Charles's manuscripts has "my sons," which he printed; see the variant.

a: the fathers of these spirits
p: The Watchers are the "fathers" of the evil spirits: demons are the giants' spirits.
b: Noah says plainly that the evil spirits troubling his family are the children of the Watchers. 1 Enoch 15:8 says the giants "will be called evil spirits on the earth." The 66 books never explain where demons come from. This goes beyond the Bible. See the card on 1 Enoch 15.

a: shut them up and hold them in the place of judgment
p: Compare the demons in Luke 8:31, who beg Jesus not to send them into the abyss.
b: Noah asks God to imprison the spirits as the Watchers were imprisoned (5:6). The idea that evil spirits fear being shut up before the time appears in the Gospels: "They kept pleading with him not to order them off into the Abyss" (Luke 8:31), and they asked, "Did you come here to torment us ahead of time?" (Matthew 8:29).

a: for you alone know their judgment
p: Charles emended to "you alone can rule over them." The Ge'ez says "know their judgment."
b: Ge'ez taʾämr kʷənänehomu, "you know their judgment." Charles changed one word so that it reads "you alone can exercise dominion over them," which fits the prayer's request. The Plain English Translation keeps the Ge'ez. Either way, Noah asks God to act because only God can deal with spirits.
orig: አንተ ባሕቲትከ ታአምር ኵነኔሆሙ (ʾäntä baḥtitkä taʾämr kʷənänehomu)

a: the chief of the spirits, Mastema
p: First appearance of Mastema. The name means "hostility." Greek writers spelled it Mastiphat; the Latin, Mastima.
b: Ge'ez mälʾäkä mänafsət, word for word "the angel of the spirits." "The chief of the spirits" is Charles's rendering, which the Plain English Translation follows because Mastema leads the spirits in 10:8-11. Charles notes the Latin form Mastima and the Greek forms Mastipham (Syncellus, who calls him "the ruler of the demons") and Mastiphat (Cedrenus). He explains the name from the Hebrew root of satan: masṭemah is "hostility" in Hosea 9:7-8, so Mastema is the equivalent of "the Satan" in meaning. In 10:11 Jubilees itself calls him Satan. Mark 3:22 speaks of "the ruler of the demons." The Plain English Translation keeps the name Mastema.

a: For if some of them are not left to me
p: As in Job 1-2, the accuser asks God's permission. God grants a tenth, not all.
b: Mastema comes before God and asks, as the Satan does in Job 1:9-12 and 2:4-6. His reason: without spirits he cannot carry out "the power of my will" among humans, whose evil is great. Charles reports that Syncellus summarized this passage: "the devil asked to take a portion of them for the testing of men," and a tenth was given him "so as to tempt men for the testing of each one's choice toward God." So the spirits left on earth serve God's purpose of testing. This goes beyond the 66 books, which never tell such a scene after the Flood, but it matches Job's picture of an accuser who acts only by God's leave.

a: Let a tenth of them remain before him
p: Claude's theory: the tenth left to Mastema mirrors the tithe, a tenth set apart.
b: This is Claude's suggestion. Jubilees cares a great deal about tithes (13:25-27; 32:1-15). Here the arithmetic is reversed: God sends nine parts to judgment and lets a tenth remain, as if the evil one were given a "tithe" of the spirits. The writer may mean that the evil left in the world is small and measured, a set portion fixed by God. No published study known to Claude makes this link; the Greek summary in Syncellus, as Charles quotes it, also has "the tenth."

a: He told one of us to teach Noah all their cures
p: Charles: the angel is Raphael, whose name means "God heals."
b: Charles reports that the Hebrew Book of Noah names the angel Raphael and makes a play on Raphael and rephuʾot, "cures." Raphael's name means "God heals." In 1 Enoch 10:7 Raphael heals the earth, and in Tobit 3:17 and 12:14-15 he is sent to cure Tobit's blindness and free Sarah from a demon.

a: to serve before Satan on the earth
p: The Ge'ez says "Satan" here, so Charles concluded Mastema and Satan are one.
b: In 10:8 the chief is Mastema; here the spirits are left "before Satan." Charles concluded that Satan and Mastema are the same. The verb yəkʷännu can mean "be subject, serve" or "carry out judgment," so the clause may also be read "to carry out judgment before Satan on the earth" (see the variant). The Plain English Translation says "serve before Satan," keeping qədmä, "before." Charles reports a parallel in the Hebrew Book of Noah: one tenth were allowed to go about on the earth "before the prince of the Mastema, to rule over the godless, to smite them and to plague them." So the spirits may serve as Satan's agents of punishment. "Satan" has a capital here because säyṭan names the figure of 10:8; in the phrase "no satan and nothing evil" later in the book it is a common noun.
orig: ከመ ይኰንኑ ቅድመ ሰይጣን (kämä yəkʷännu qədmä säyṭan)

a: so that he could heal with the plants of the earth
p: Noah learns to cure the demons' diseases with plants. The Bible elsewhere honors physicians and medicine.
b: Jubilees treats illness as partly the work of evil spirits and medicine as a gift taught by angels. The Bible does not say that angels taught medicine, but it does use remedies: Isaiah's fig poultice for Hezekiah (Isaiah 38:21), the "balm in Gilead" (Jeremiah 8:22), and Sirach's praise of the physician (Sirach 38:1-8). Charles thought the writer here "falls away" from his own high teaching into something like Tobit's fish-liver remedy (Tobit 6:7-8). This goes beyond the 66 books.

a: Noah wrote down in a book
p: Jubilees speaks of a book written by Noah. A Hebrew Book of Noah of the Middle Ages knows the same story.
b: Charles notes that the medieval Hebrew Book of Noah keeps much of verses 1-2 and 9-14 (it is printed in Jellinek's Bet ha-Midrasch and in Charles's 1895 edition). It begins a book of medical lore. Whether there was an ancient "Book of Noah" that Jubilees used, or whether the later book drew on Jubilees, scholars debate.

a: He gave all the books he had written to Shem, his oldest son
p: Noah's books go to Shem. Later Jacob gives all his books to Levi (45:16).
b: Charles notes that Shem receives the books as the eldest son or as the priest of the family. The book builds a chain of written teaching: Enoch writes (4:17-19), Noah writes, Shem keeps the books, and at the end Jacob gives all the books to Levi (45:16), the priestly tribe. The claim is that Israel's priests hold an unbroken written tradition going back before the Flood.

a: nineteen jubilees, two weeks of years and five years
p: 19 jubilees (931) + 2 weeks (14) + 5 years = 950 years, as in Genesis 9:29.
b: Genesis 9:29: "All of Noah's days came to 950 years, and he died." Jubilees gives the same total in its own units: nineteen jubilees of 49 years (931), two weeks of years (14) and five years. Charles notes a small strain in the book's dates: by 6:18 Noah dies in year 1659, which with 950 years puts his birth in 709, not the 707 that other dates imply.

a: all except Enoch
p: Only Enoch surpasses Noah, because Enoch keeps the record for the judgment.
b: In 4:23-24 Jubilees says the angels led Enoch into Eden, where he writes down the judgment of the world. Charles calls him the scribe of God. Here Enoch's "work" is to report the deeds of every generation "on the day of judgment." 1 Enoch 12:3-4 calls Enoch "the scribe of righteousness." Genesis says only that "God took him" (Genesis 5:24).

a: he named him Reu
p: Charles: the name Reu was heard as Hebrew raʿ, "evil."
b: The Ge'ez spells the name Ragaw, and Charles notes the Greek form Ragau. Charles explains the reason given as a Hebrew pun: Reu (Reʿu) sounds like "they have become evil" (raʿu). Lomna and Sinaor are names found only here; Charles notes the Syriac list of wives has Lomna.

a: Let's go up by it into heaven
p: In Genesis the builders want a tower "with its head in the heavens." Here they want to climb into heaven.
b: Genesis 11:4: "Come on, let's build ourselves a city, and a tower with its head in the heavens." Jubilees makes the aim plainer: to "go up by it into heaven." Charles compares Epiphanius. Many ancient readers took the tower as an attack on heaven itself.

a: asphalt that comes out of the sea
p: Genesis 11:3 has "bitumen to use as mortar." Jubilees says where it came from.
b: Genesis 11:3: "They had brick to use as stone and bitumen to use as mortar." The Ge'ez has ʾasfalitos, from Greek asphaltos, a sign of the Greek translation behind the Ge'ez. Bitumen seeps from the ground in Mesopotamia and floats on the Dead Sea. Charles notes that the Chronicles of Jerahmeel seem to draw on this verse.

a: They built it for forty-three years
p: The Ge'ez numbers are hard. A Greek quotation gives 43 years, 203 bricks broad, 13 stades.
b: Charles quotes the Greek of the Catena of Nicephorus: "For 43 years they remained building. The height was 8,000 cubits and two spans, the breadth 203 bricks. The height of the brick was one-third of one brick. The length of one wall was 13 stadia." The Ge'ez numerals read word for word "five hundreds, four hundreds, thirty, three" (ኀምሳ ምእት ወአርባዕቱ ምእት ወሠላሳ ወሠላስ (ḫämsa məʾt wäʾärbaʿtu məʾt wäśälasa wäśälas)) cubits. The Plain English Translation gives 5,433, the figure of Charles's English; how the words yield that number is not plain from the Ge'ez alone. A cubit is about 18 inches. Charles emended three small points to make sense of the verse. Jerome knew this verse: he says the Hebrew word rissah occurs, as far as he remembered, only in "the apocryphal book which the Greeks call Leptē Genesis," as a word for a stadium.

a: Come, let us go down
p: Here God speaks to the angels: "us" means God and his angels.
b: Genesis 11:7: "Come, let us go down and mix up their language there." Readers have long asked who "us" is. Jubilees answers: God speaks to the angels of the presence, who then go down "with him" (10:23). Jewish readers often took Genesis' "let us" the same way; many Christian readers, from the church fathers on, saw in it a hint of the Trinity.

a: Babel
p: Genesis 11:9 links Babel with Hebrew balal, "mix." Jubilees keeps the explanation.
b: Genesis 11:9: "That is how the place got the name Babel, because it was there that the LORD mixed up the speech of all the earth." The name sounds like Hebrew balal, "mix, confuse." Jubilees uses "God" (ʾAmlak) here, where Genesis has the LORD.

a: The Lord sent a wind against the tower and threw it down
p: Genesis never says the tower fell. Jubilees has a wind throw it down.
b: In Genesis the builders simply stop (Genesis 11:8). Charles calls the wind "a very old tradition," found also in the Sibylline Oracles (3:98-103), Josephus (Antiquities 1.4.3), Epiphanius and the Byzantine chroniclers. The name "Overthrow" (Ge'ez dəqät) differs from Genesis' "Babel"; Charles thinks the Hebrew had a play on words lost in Ge'ez. This goes beyond Genesis.

a: Canaan saw that the land of Lebanon, as far as the Brook of Egypt, was very good
p: Jubilees explains why the land was called "Canaan": Canaan squatted in Shem's portion.
b: Canaan's own lot lay in the far west, by the sea, which Charles took to be north-west Africa (9:1). But he saw the land "from Lebanon to the River of Egypt" and stayed there. The phrase echoes the borders of the promised land (Numbers 34:5; 1 Kings 8:65, "from Lebo-hamath down to the Brook of Egypt"). Charles notes that Syncellus later told the same story: Canaan, "acting seditiously," stepped onto Shem's borders, and God gave the land back to Israel through Moses and Joshua. For the book's first readers this answered a hard question about the conquest. See the chapter page.

a: through rebellion your children will fall
p: Ge'ez hakak, "sedition, turmoil": Canaan's settlement is an act of rebellion against the oath.
b: Charles compares Syncellus's Greek neōterisas, "having acted seditiously." The word is repeated three times in the verse: by rebellion Canaan settled, by rebellion he will be cursed, and by rebellion his children will fall. The curse of 9:14 comes into force.

a: the holy judge
p: Charles: the angel present at the drawing of lots (8:10).
b: Ge'ez mäkʷännən qədus. Charles takes the "holy judge" to be the angel who stayed with Noah's sons when they cast lots (8:10). Some readers take it as God himself, who is "the righteous judge" in 5:16.

a: from Hamath to the entrance of Egypt
p: Hamath to Egypt: the old biblical limits of Israel's land.
b: Hamath (Ge'ez ʾEmat) was Israel's northern limit (Numbers 34:8). Charles cites 2 Chronicles 7:8, where the gathering comes "from Lebo-hamath down to the Brook of Egypt." "To this day" speaks from the time of Moses, to whom the angel tells the story.

a: That is why that land is called the land of Canaan
t: The land named for a thief
p: In Genesis the land is simply Canaan's. In Jubilees it carries the name of the one who stole it.
b: Genesis 10:15-19 gives the Canaanites' borders without comment. Jubilees makes the very name "the land of Canaan" a reminder of a broken oath. This goes beyond Genesis. Genesis 15:16 gives a different reason for the later conquest: "the guilt of the Amorites is not yet full."

a: saw the land of the sea, and he did not like it
p: Jubilees explains why the Medes lived in Shem's part of the world.
b: Media lay east of Assyria, among peoples Jubilees counts as Shem's. So the book has Madai ask his wife's brothers for land. Charles notes that Diodorus of Antioch seems to have known this story: he read Genesis 9:27 ("may he live in the tents of Shem") as fulfilled when Madai, the Mede, took "the most beautiful part" of Shem's dwelling. The Ge'ez spells Media Medqin. Unlike Canaan, Madai asked and received; he did not seize.
